title: Just do it. (let your tools think for themselves) - Robert Chandler

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central subject is MCP tool design, arguing for agentic tools over low-level API wrappers. Wordware is a developer platform for building agents, and the MCP patterns discussed apply cross-domain. Covers development patterns for building agentic tools and production reliability problems with agent tool use. Assumes familiarity with MCP, LLM agents, and tool-calling patterns. summary: Robert Chandler, co-founder and CTO at Wordware, draws on experience from self-driving cars and helping hundreds of teams build reliable AI agents. He argues that the promise of agents—automated systems taking real-world action with full context—is undermined when MCPs are thin wrappers around low-level APIs not designed for language models. Such wrappers produce messy JSON that pollutes context, offer tiny single-function scopes requiring long chains of calls, demand painful authentication, and flood the context window with tool definitions—Slack alone adds eight tools, Notion adds twenty. His core thesis is to add more agency to tools rather than making them small. Using an Avengers analogy, he advocates specialized agents instead of an Inspector Gadget with a thousand tiny tools. The goal is to blur the line between tool and agent, giving agents tidy natural language APIs that produce reliable, reusable, high-quality outputs. He demonstrates Wordware's new MCP toolbox, which lets users turn Wordware programs into agentic MCP tools. He shows a competitor analysis flow integrating Twitter scraping and Notion output, with detailed prompts encoding taste and reasoning. Connecting this toolbox to Claude, he runs a competitor analysis for Anthropic AI, producing a formatted Notion page summarizing Anthropic's Twitter style. He emphasizes that multiple tools can be grouped into toolboxes and toggled per task, enabling a generic agent to offload complex work to a specialized, reliable sub-agent—mirroring how human teams delegate to specialists.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Low-level MCP wrappers around APIs fail because they pollute agent context with JSON blobs and force LLMs to reason over long chains of function calls
Adding more tools increases noise exponentially—Slack MCP adds 8 tools, Notion adds 20—making it hard for agents to perform reliably
The solution is to make tools agentic: blur the line between agent and tool, give sub-agents natural language APIs that return clean outputs
Agentic MCPs act like specialized team members (Avengers analogy) rather than tiny function wrappers (Inspector Gadget analogy)
Wordware's MCP toolbox lets you turn Wordware programs into agentic MCP tools callable by other agents like Claude
A demonstrated competitor analysis tool integrated Twitter scraping and Notion output, producing a formatted summary with reliable, repeatable results
Multiple tools can be grouped into toolboxes and toggled on or off per task, reducing context pollution
A Slack MCP example wasted 5 minutes and failed to send a simple message, posting to a general channel instead of the intended recipient
Generic agents can offload complex, taste-driven tasks to specialized sub-agents for aligned, high-quality results
Understand why low-level API wrappers as MCPs fail for agent use

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Robert Chandler introduces himself as co-founder and CTO at Wordware, where he has helped hundreds of teams build reliable AI agents. He previously worked on self-driving cars, emphasizing high-reliability systems.

sections.title: Promise vs Reality of Agents and Slack MCP Example
sections.summary: Agents promise automated real-world action with full context, but are often slow, expensive, and unreliable. A Slack MCP example failed to send a simple message to Philip, instead listing users and channels and resorting to posting in general, taking 5 minutes.

sections.title: Problems with Low-Level MCP Wrappers
sections.summary: Low-level MCPs pollute context with JSON blobs, have tiny single-function scopes requiring long call chains, demand painful authentication, and add too many tools (Slack 8, Notion 20). Multi-tool pagination further degrades LLM reasoning over longer chains.

sections.title: Solution: Agentic Tools
sections.summary: Chandler advocates adding agency to tools rather than making them small. Using an Avengers analogy, he proposes specialized agents over tiny function wrappers. The goal is to blur the line between tool and agent, giving sub-agents tidy natural language APIs for reliable outputs.

sections.title: Wordware MCP Toolbox Demonstration
sections.summary: Demonstrates Wordware's new MCP toolbox for building agentic MCPs. A competitor analysis Wordware integrates Twitter scraping and Notion output with detailed prompts. The toolbox connects to Claude, and multiple tools can be grouped and toggled per task.

sections.title: Results and Conclusion
sections.summary: The competitor analysis for Anthropic AI produces a formatted Notion page summarizing Anthropic's Twitter style. Chandler concludes that blurring the line between agent and tool lets generic agents offload complex tasks to specialized, reliable sub-agents, mirroring human team delegation.
